name: Thai Basil Chicken (Pad Krapow)
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Saucy stir-fry with zero unmapped ingredients - oyster-sauce, fish-sauce, soy-sauce and fresh-basil are all tracked commodities. Wok-style but not fried-to-order: it is a stir-and-simmer that holds in a hotel pan and portions over rice. No basil stir-fry live. Confidence: MEDIUM - URL confirmed on the site's own search index, page not individually fetched. | HARVEST: Published nutrition excludes the rice.
intro_html: Pad krapow is the dish Thai people actually eat on a Tuesday. Chicken and chile and garlic hit a screaming hot pan, a sauce of oyster and soy goes in, and then an absurd amount of basil gets folded through at the last second so it wilts but never cooks. Five minutes of cooking, a lifetime of craving it afterward. Over rice, each bowl runs {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein for about ${{cost_ps}} (at everyday cost). That price is higher than it looks like it should be, and I will show you exactly why.
ingredients_display: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh (Member's Mark): 3.5 lb (1575 g)
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh, 3.5 lb: ~$11.18. Buy 4 lbs: $12.88.
Rice, 6.75 cups dry: ~$1.48. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 2 2lb bags.
Pantry seasonings (salt, black pepper): ~$0.17. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $30.98 across 14 servings, so roughly $2.21 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $34.47 across 14 servings, roughly $2.46 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $13.09 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $47.56. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a bowl (at everyday cost), and here is the honest accounting: the basil costs more than the chicken. Seven cups of fresh basil is what makes this pad krapow rather than a generic stir fry, so it is worth the money, but it is the line to attack if you want this cheaper.
shop_smart: Basil is the largest line in this batch, larger than the meat. Buy a living basil plant from the produce section instead of clamshells and you will pay a fraction of the price, or grow one on a windowsill and this recipe becomes one of the cheapest things you make all month.
Thai holy basil is the traditional leaf and Italian sweet basil is the one your store stocks. Either one works. Do not pay a premium for a specialty basil shipped in from three states away.
Oyster sauce and soy sauce are pantry buys that last months and cost pennies per batch. One bottle of each covers a dozen recipes on this site.
Boneless thighs beat breast here because the pan is hot and fast and thighs forgive a few extra seconds. The four pound club pack is the best price in the case.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Whisk the oyster sauce, soy sauce and sugar together in a small bowl with a splash of water. Have it standing by, because once this cooks there is no time to measure anything.
Chop the chicken thighs into small pieces, roughly the size of a thumbnail, so they cook through in the time a stir fry allows.
Cook the rice first and let it steam covered off the heat while you do everything else.
Heat the vegetable oil in your largest skillet or wok over the highest heat you have. Add the minced garlic and sliced jalapeno and cook 20 seconds, just until the garlic turns pale gold.

Add the chicken in batches so the pan never cools down and stir hard for 4 to 5 minutes until it is cooked through and browned in spots, seasoning with the salt and black pepper as it cooks. Crowding the pan is the one mistake that ruins this dish.
Return all the chicken to the pan, pour in the sauce, and let it bubble and reduce for a minute until it clings to the meat.
Kill the heat, throw in the fresh basil and the sliced green onions all at once, and fold until the basil just wilts. Then combine with the rice in your mixing pot.
portion_html: Set the pot on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight, and divide by 14. Same number in every container. Each one carries {{cal}} calories, and if you want it to taste freshly made on day four, stir a few torn basil leaves in after reheating.

recipeIngredient: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh, 3.5 lb (1575 g)
steps: Whisk oyster sauce, soy sauce and sugar with a splash of water and set the sauce aside.
Cook the rice and steam it covered off the heat.
Sizzle garlic and jalapeno in very hot oil for 20 seconds, then stir fry the chopped chicken in batches 4 to 5 minutes, seasoning with salt and black pepper.
Return all the chicken, add the sauce, and reduce a minute until it clings.
Fold in the basil and green onions off the heat, combine with the rice, and portion into 14 containers.
